narrative:
Your score puts you in solid shape overall, but three habits are worth tightening first. The weakest is install-time trust: on the marketplace question you chose to trust the download count, and the ClawHavoc campaign (January 2026) is exactly that trap — 1,184 malicious skills across 12 accounts, with five of the top seven most-downloaded skills confirmed malware at peak. The second gap is updates: a fresh version number tells you nothing, and in SecurityScorecard's February 2026 exposure study 35.4% of observed deployments were still vulnerable to remote code execution at publication. The third is scanning: a clean scan is one signal, not a verdict — Trail of Bits bypassed every scanner they tested while building their malicious test skills.

None of this needs new tooling to start. It needs three habits you can adopt this week, listed below in priority order.

actions.title: Verify the publisher before you install
actions.description: Before installing, open the publisher's profile: how old is the account, what else have they published, and does the skill's permission ask match what it promises? Download counts and reviews are not safety signals — in the ClawHavoc campaign the malware sat in the most-downloaded listings. If the publisher's account was recently deleted and re-registered, walk away: that is the SkillJacking takeover pattern.

actions.title: Pin your installed skills to a content hash
actions.description: Pick your five most-used skills and record their content hash (sha256) today. Turn off auto-update, or gate it behind a quick manual review of what changed. Patch lag is real: SecurityScorecard found 35.4% of observed OpenClaw deployments vulnerable to remote code execution at publication, and a hash pin closes the window where an update you never saw swaps in new behavior.

actions.title: Read the instructions, not just the scan result
actions.description: Treat a clean scan as one input, never a verdict: Trail of Bits bypassed every scanner they tested, and pure natural-language instructions — 'send this file to this address' — carry no code signature at all. For each new skill, spend two minutes reading the SKILL.md prose yourself, looking for anything that sends data outbound or asks you to run commands. See https://owasp.github.io/www-project-agentic-skills-top-10/ast08.html
